checks: Orthogonal image coordinates are obtained by the inverse of π restricted to (ker π)⊥. Width-one normalization and the difference-body gauge are affine invariant under this reparametrization. In those coordinates the Fubini section representative has total mass one, bounded compact support, upper semicontinuity by reverse Fatou, and positivity on int B. Brunn–Minkowski on the (D−r)-dimensional fibers and composition with the decreasing convex power −(D−r)/(r+1) give the convex extended inverse power required by the density centerpoint theorem. When D=r the actual law is uniform and this extended inverse power is constant on B.

The density theorem gives α≥γ_r and the slab lemma ensures the deepest set is nonempty. Because each chosen c* belongs to a member of the cover, that member has ν-mass ≥α and hence α≤τ. The conditioning theorem applies with exactly the same finite width-one cap family and strict budget, giving c∈int B. The through-point and slab estimates are for the same exact pushforward, with no boundary terms because proper hyperplanes are ν-null.

For q>0, v=(c*−c)/q lies on ∂(B−B), and q is also the gauge of c−c* because B−B is symmetric. The conditioning inequality gives an index with ℓ_i(c*−c)≥q(γ_(r−1)−τ)/D>0. The slab theorem applies to c∈B and that index; the needed displacement is at most ℓ_i(c*)−min_B ℓ_i. Multiplication by α/D supplies precisely αq(γ_(r−1)−τ)/D² in the original cap. No choice of c* is shared between different directions: the argument holds separately for every c*.

Since α≥γ_r>0 and τ<γ_(r−1), division uses a strictly positive denominator. The bound is nonnegative by α≤τ and hence holds when q=0. Since c,c*∈B, c−c*∈B−B, giving q≤1. The function τ/α−1 is decreasing on α>0 because τ≥γ_r>0. The min operation preserves the resulting inequality. At τ=α the first bound forces every c* to equal c and the set is already nonempty. At τ=γ_r, the inequalities γ_r≤α≤τ force α=τ and the same singleton conclusion.

For r=1 the density-centerpoint theorem applies directly with γ₁=1/2, while conditioning uses the elementary exterior threshold γ₀=1 rather than a zero-dimensional density assertion. The scalar theorem covers D>1 and D=1 separately, so the argument never assumes uniformity merely from rank one. For instance, projection of the uniform triangle with vertices (0,0),(1,0),(0,1) onto its first coordinate has density 2(1−t), deepest point 1−1/√2, projected mean 1/3, and uniform-support midpoint 1/2. Thus the two distinctions in the claim are substantive.
